title: Why Windows came with Solitaire
hook: A card game was quietly teaching millions of people how to use a mouse.
peek: Windows 3.0 came with Solitaire in 1990. It looked like a way to waste time at work, but it had a job to do: getting people who had only ever typed at a keyboard to click, drag and drop.
lede: When Windows 3.0 arrived in 1990, many office workers had never used a mouse. Their computers had run on typed commands. Microsoft included a version of Klondike Solitaire, written by an intern, and dragging cards around the screen turned out to be a painless way to practise pointing, clicking and dragging without reading a manual.

bullets.text: Wes Cherry wrote the game in his spare time during a Microsoft internship around 1988. He was not paid royalties, despite it ending up on hundreds of millions of computers, and has joked about it in interviews since.

The card faces were drawn by Susan Kare, the designer behind many of the original Macintosh icons. Several of the best-known backs, including the castle, the beach and the robot, are credited to Cherry's then-girlfriend, Leslie Kooy.
Winning set off a cascade of cards bouncing across the screen, leaving trails behind them. For many people it was their first sight of a computer doing animation just for fun.
Windows 3.1 added Minesweeper in 1992, which gave the same kind of practice for a different skill: using the right mouse button, which marks a square with a flag, and clicking quickly and precisely.
